items.title: Clair Obscur Officially Drops Long-Awaited New Release Coming November 2026
items.summary: Clair Obscur's Esquie is a fan-favorite character, and now, he's returning with a brand-new release this year.
items.content:
Image via Sandfall Interactive By Emma Singer Published Aug 20, 2026, 11:00 PM EDT Emma Singer is an Anime & Gaming Editor from New York with over two years of experience writing about media for CBR. Outside of writing, Emma enjoys doing yoga, and playing golf and tennis. Sign in to your CBR account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Listen Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 surprised everyone in 2025. The turn-based RPG from indie studio Sandfall Interactive blew past expectations, selling 8 million copies and winning Game of the Year at The Game Awards. It's already considered a modern classic, and while players are still waiting on a follow-up, a new Esquie release is coming later this year.

While Esquie isn't one of the main characters of Clair Obscur , he's become a fan-favorite. He might look like a giant toy , but he's one of the most powerful characters in the game's universe, and he plays a surprising role in Clair Obscur 's story. Now, fans can bring Esquie home with a new release from Nendoroid.

Image via Good Smile Company With Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 being such a massive hit, it was always going to end up receiving merchandise. Now, fans of the RPG have the chance to purchase a statue of one of the game's most beloved characters, Esquie.

The new figure is from Nendoroid, one of the biggest names in toys and statues based on anime and video games. Esquie is an adorably designed mythical creature with a pure soul that captured the hearts of fans everywhere, and many people have been waiting for a figure like this since the game released last year.

Pre-orders for "Nendoroid Esquie" are already closed on Goodsmile, but are still available from select retailers. Fans of Clair Obscur will need to act quickly if they want to bring this collectible home. Statues will then be shipped out sometime in November. The "Nendoroid Esquie" is available for 7,800￥ JPY, or approximately $46 USD.

"Nendoroid Esquie" is a non-scale articulated statue that comes with a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 branded stand. It's approximately 102mm in height, it can be made to pose in a variety of ways, and it's made from plastic. Perhaps most fun, Esquie can be equipped with a removable headband and hold his rough-around-the-edges tortoise best friend, François.

Surprisingly, the official description for "Nendoroid Esquie" is surprisingly sparse for a statue of its kind. It merely says, "Bonjour, mes amis!" an instantly identifiable quote of Esquie's which roughly translates from French to, "Hello, my friends!" Given the popularity of the character, it seems that no other description was deemed necessary.

For Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 fans who are more interested in new gaming experiences than a wholesome, adorable statue, no worry is necessary. Sandfall Interactive also released a one-year anniversary update in April, which allows players to give their characters new haircuts, play with photo mode, and take on "Verso's Drafts."

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is currently available on PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series X/S, and PC.

items.title: Ex-PlayStation Boss Told Expedition 33 Devs To Avoid Calling It A Turn-Based RPG To Attract More Gamers
items.summary: Shuhei Yoshida advised the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 team that labeling the game a turn-based RPG might cause players to overlook it. The studio instead promoted its "reactive turn-based battles."

The studio instead promoted its "reactive turn-based battles." News By GBest - Aug 20, 2026 05:08 PM EST Filed Under: Role-Playing Former PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida once advised the developers of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 not to market the game as a turn-based RPG. Speaking at the Busan Indie Connect Festival in 2026, Yoshida recalled warning the team that the label alone could cause some players to dismiss the game before giving it a chance.

Yoshida played an early demo of the game roughly two years before its release while working in an advisory role with publisher Kepler Interactive. He was impressed by the combat, which combines traditional turn-based structure with real-time timing elements for dodges, parries, and counters. He compared the system favorably to The Legend of Dragoon , a game he produced during his time at Sony.

Despite his enthusiasm, Yoshida believed the broader perception of turn-based JRPGs at the time worked against the project. “It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG,” he said. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

Sandfall Interactive and Kepler took the advice to heart. In marketing materials the game was frequently described as featuring "reactive turn-based battles" rather than simply a turn-based RPG. The phrasing emphasized the active, timing-based layer that sets the combat apart from more traditional implementations of the genre.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 went on to become one of the most successful debut RPGs in recent years, earning widespread critical praise and strong sales. Its combat system, which rewards precise defensive inputs during enemy turns while still allowing strategic planning on the player’s turn, has been singled out as a major reason for its appeal. Many players who might have skipped a conventional turn-based RPG engaged with the game because of how the battles actually played.

Yoshida shared the anecdote as part of a broader discussion about how indie developers should pitch their games to publishers and present them to audiences. His point was that genre labels carry assumptions, and sometimes those assumptions can limit a game’s reach even when the underlying design is strong. In the case of Expedition 33 , adjusting the language helped frame the combat as something more dynamic and modern without changing the systems themselves.

The story also reflects how perceptions of turn-based games have shifted. What was viewed as potentially outdated a few years ago has seen renewed interest, partly because of titles like Expedition 33 that prove the style still has room to evolve. Yoshida’s advice captured a specific moment in the market. The game’s later success suggests the caution was understandable at the time, even if the final result showed there was a sizable audience ready for a well-executed take on the genre.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 stands as a clear example of a project that benefited from careful positioning. By avoiding a label that some players associated with slower or more traditional experiences, the team gave the game a better chance to be judged on its actual combat and presentation rather than preconceptions about the genre.

What are your thoughts on the comment and advice? Do you think it paid off for them? Did it really matter? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below!

items.content:

That wasn't the case just a few years ago, when former PlayStation boss Shuhei Yoshida advised Sandfall Interactive to avoid describing Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, now among the most awarded games of all time , as a turn-based JRPG for fear that it "might lost the interest of many consumers." These days, Yoshida finds the irony of that advice in hindsight amusing.

"I advised them that if they described the game as a turn-based JRPG, they might lose the interest of many consumers," Yoshida tells GamerBraves . "I suggested that they come up with a new name for the combat system."

Without wading into the interminable debate around what makes a JRPG a JRPG , I'll just say objectively that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 isn't strictly a JRPG because Sandfall is a French developer, but it largely fits the bill from a gameplay perspective despite a unique combat system labeled "reactive" turn-based, apparently based on Yoshida's suggestion.

Nowadays, "A lot of developers are now pitching new turn-based JRPG-like games to publishers. So, it's really funny," he says.

Somewhat ironically, there actually isn't a single turn-based RPG having released or about to release in 2026 that's really defining the zeitgeist in the way Clair Obscur or Baldur's Gate 3 did during their respective release years, but with Larian's new Divinity confirmed to be a turn-based RPG and Persona 6 on the horizon, that's bound to change eventually.

items.title: Shuhei Yoshida told Expedition 33 studio to avoid terms like 'turn-based RPG' because it may cause people to "overlook" the game
items.summary: The perceived negative stigma around the term 'turn-based RPG' has led Shuhei Yoshida to advise Expedition 33 developers to avoid using it.
items.content:
Image credit: Sandfall / Eurogamer News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Aug. 18, 2026, 8:29 a.m. 37 comments Follow Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 One of the reasons Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 stood out so much in early footage was how action-packed its combat looked, despite being a turn-based RPG. But while developer Sandfall Interactive has described the game as a turn-based RPG - and reinvigorated the genre, to some degree - not everyone was happy with that approach.

Veteran PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida revealed at the Busan Indie Connect Festival 2026 over the weekend that he warned Expedition 33 developers not to give the game that label (via Automaton ).

Yoshida was impressed by the game's combat, likening it to The Legend of Dragoon's, a game he was the producer of. However, his advice was for the team to pick a different term to describe the game, since he believed 'turn-based RPG' is an outdated term to some players, who could end up dismissing the game as a result.

"It's incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG. That alone might cause players to overlook it," Yoshida said, as reported by 4Gamer .

Yoshida, who worked as an advisor to publishers and developers around the time of his departure from PlayStation in 2025 , revealed the anecdote in a panel aimed at helping indie developers pick the right publisher for their games and making a convincing pitch. As part of his consulting work, he worked with Expedition 33 publisher Kepler Interactive, where he got to play a demo of the game two years before its launch.

According to the report, Kepler and Sandfall took his advice, using the more modern 'reactive turn-based battles' term to describe the game's combat instead. As anyone who played the game will attest, Expedition 33's brand of turn-based combat, which melds real-time mechanics like parrying and dodging with traditional turn orders, became one of the strongest and most-lauded aspects of the game .

Regardless of how much you think Yoshida's advice helped, the success of the game is hard to deny. Expedition 33 initially managed to sell a fitting 3.3 million copies in its first month , before bumping that to 5.5 million copies by October 2025.

It's also been one of the highest-rated games of 2025, winning multiple honours at The Game Awards that year, and ending up at number two on Eurogamer's list of the 50 best games of 2025 .

items.title: 'It's Incredibly Well-Made, But…' — Former PlayStation Boss Warned Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Devs It Would Be 'Overlooked' if They Called It a Turn-Based RPG
items.summary: Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it.
items.content:
Former PlayStation lead Shuhei Yoshida warned the developers behind Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 about calling it a "turn-based RPG" because "that alone might cause players to overlook it."

Yoshida, who served as PlayStation's head of indies and president of Sony Interactive Entertainment Worldwide Studios before stepping down in 2024, spoke about some key advice he gave the award-winning team during a recent lecture for indie game developers. Portions of that lecture were then reported by 4Gamer and subsequently translated by Automaton , including one piece of advice he gave to publisher Kepler Interactive while advising the team ahead of its April 2025 launch.

"It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG," Yoshida warned the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 devs. "That alone might cause players to overlook it."

But why? Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 went on to receive praise from fans and critics (including a 9/10 review from IGN), while ending its already explosive year with big wins across The Game Awards , BAFTA , DICE , and IGN award shows. Its positive reception was so intense that even the developers at Sandfall Interactive weren't prepared for its towering Metacritic score .

Yoshida acknowledged Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 as a quality release long before it reached the hands of the public. He was impressed early on, calling attention to its "combination of turn-based JRPG mechanics and real-time action inputs reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon." The problem, however, was that, at the time, he was concerned its success could be affected by what he observed to be a tendency for turn-based JRPGs to be seen as outdated.

Game-award-winning formula or not, Yoshida feared Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 would be ignored by some gamers if they saw that "turn-based" label. As a result, Kepler got creative and instead started selling Sandfall's first game as an experience with "reactive turn-based battles" instead, and the rest is history.

The game, of course, went on to become a massive sales success despite its proximity to the launch of The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion . Yoshida said he's since noticed an uptick in reports from publishers receiving pitches for new turn-based RPGs.

While we wait to see what's next from Yoshida and Sandfall, you can see why the developers behind Final Fantasy Resonance think turn-based RPGs are making a huge comeback . You can also read the devs' conversation about canon endings and the writer who got their start at Sandfall .

Michael Cripe is a freelance writer with IGN. He's best known for his work at sites like The Pitch, The Escapist, and OnlySP. Be sure to give him a follow on Bluesky (@mikecripe.bsky.social) and Twitter (@MikeCripe).

items.title: Shuhei Yoshida advised Expedition 33 developers not to call it a "turn-based RPG" due to negative JRPG stigma at the time
items.summary: Yoshida recalled the anecdote during a lecture to indie developers on pitching their games to publishers.
items.content:
Home News Shuhei Yoshida advised Expedition 33 developers not to call it a “turn-based RPG” due to negative JRPG stigma at the time Yoshida recalled the anecdote during a lecture to indie developers on pitching their games to publishers.

Game Development , News 2026-08-17 22:00 Amber V 21 During the Busan Indie Connect Festival 2026 held in South Korea from August 14 to 16, former PlayStation executive Shuhei Yoshida held a lecture to indie game developers, offering insight on how to choose a publisher and successfully pitch your game (as reported by 4Gamer ). As part of the presentation, Yoshida also cited anecdotes from his own career as an advisor to publishers, including Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 publisher Kepler Interactive.

When asked how much game publishers care about chasing trends, Yoshida says that, in his experience, it tends to depend on whether the specific publisher picks up games that are nearly finished, or spends several years building projects from scratch. The former is often mindful of pursuing trends, while the latter is not – given that whatever is trendy at the moment is anyhow bound to be outdated by the time of launch.

Yoshida illustrates this point with an episode from the development of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. As an advisor to Kepler Interactive, Yoshida played a demo of the game about two years prior to its launch. He was immediately impressed by the combat, which he describes as a “combination of turn-based JRPG mechanics and real-time action inputs reminiscent of The Legend of Dragoon” (which he was the producer of).

However, despite being personally impressed by the gameplay, Yoshida observed a tendency for turn-based JRPGs to be dismissed as outdated at the time, so he advised the developers at Sandfall Interactive not to label it as one. “It’s incredibly well-made, but it would be better not to call it a turn-based RPG. That alone might cause players to overlook it.” Consequently, the branding was adjusted to terms like “reactive turn-based battles.”

After Expedition 33 became a breakout hit, Yoshida says, publishers have apparently started receiving a steady stream of pitches for turn-based RPGs. He sees this story as a prime example of success not being guaranteed just by pursuing market trends.

items.title: The "untranslatable" book that inspired Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has been translated, and you can buy it later this year
items.summary: La Horde du Contrevent (or: Horde of the Counterwind) is available in hardback later this year.
items.content:
Image credit: Eurogamer News by Dom Peppiatt Deputy Editorial Director Published on Aug. 12, 2026, 3:46 p.m. 9 comments Follow Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 The first ever English translation of Alain Damasio’s Horde of the Counterwind (or, to give the book its original name La Horde du Contrevent) is going on sale later this year. The novel, a cult classic that is cited as one of the driving inspirations behind the acclaimed and best-selling Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , will be available in hardback on 13th October, 2026 via Abrams Books in the US. The UK date seems to be listed as 12th November on Amazon ; we have contacted the publisher for clarification.

"Follow a horde of hardened expeditioners as they climb endlessly against the wind that plagues their desolate homeland," reads a blurb for the book. "Their only purpose: to make it to the Upper Reaches and identify the wind's mysterious source. Over the course of eight hundred years, thirty-three hordes before them have tried and failed."

Similarly to the game, the 2004 book focuses on loss, grief, and unending perseverance in the face of almost impossible odds. Awarded the Grand Prix de l’Imaginaire 2006 in the category "Francophone novel", it quickly became a cult hit amongst French-language speakers, and is considered a modern classic in sci-fi today.

The book has long been considered impossible to translate thanks to the intricacies and uniqueness of its prose, but poet, novelist, translator and literary scholar Alexander Dickow is giving it a damn good go for the sake of English audiences. He's got some pretty good credits, too: to date, Dickow has translated The Central Laboratory by Max Jacob, The Neverending Quest for the Other Shore by Sylvie Kandé, Showers and Bright Spells: Selected Poems 2009–2019 by Henri Droguet, and Air of Solitude and Requiem by Gustave Roud (the last two were co-translated with Sean T. Reynolds, but I think that oeuvre more than paints a picture of Dickow's tastes and talents).

Before Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 launched in 2025, Sandfall Interactive co-founder and chief technology officer Tom Guillermin told Unreal that Damasio’s book was one of the inspirations for the game: "On the story side, there is also a French novel called ‘La Horde du Contrevent’, which is a fantasy novel about a group of explorers travelling the world, which our game also took some inspiration from as we made a story about people venturing into the unknown on a dangerous adventure," he told the blog .

The novel is cited as a major inspiration for the hit RPG alongside the Belle Époque era of European history, an unnamed painting that struck something inside game director Guillaume Broche, and video games like Persona, Final Fantasy, and Lost Odyssey . "All these influences (and many more) helped shape our original vision for the game and develop something that feels completely unique for players," Guillermin concluded.

This book has been on my StoryGraph 'to read' column for a while now, so I'm pleased we finally get a chance to read it in English later this year. I'll be checking it out when it launches, and - having completed Expedition 33 twice, now - I plan to write up what I learn about the game's narrative inspirations when I'm done. I hope you're all as excited as I am about this book finally making its way to our shores. Tomorrow comes.

items.title: 1 year later, the best Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 quote still lives rent-free in my head
items.content:
on Google Preferred Source Google News Link copied to clipboard By Rebecca Corgan Published Aug 7, 2026, 1:30 PM EDT FYI ‘Wheee’ balances ‘whooo’ is still so true

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Sign in to your Polygon.com account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Getting through an average day in 2026 requires resilience – the basic ability to weather mundane-but-constant highs, like a good news text from a friend, and lows, like realizing you need to head to the store (again) to pick up an item you forgot (again). Achieving that ability to manage everything going on at once is hard. It’s tempting to allow yourself to ricochet from high to low in rollercoaster fashion – but we need to give our brains a break. We must…achieve…balance.

Easier said than done, of course. So let’s work to avoid burnout, take a deep breath in and out, and remember the immortal words of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 ’s Esquie: “I too am ‘Whooo.’ But I’m also ‘Wheee!’ So the ‘Wheee’ balances the ‘Whooo.’”

Image: Sandfall Interactive/Kepler Interactive via Polygon Esquie’s mantra, here, comes from one of the many camp conversations you can enjoy during downtime in an otherwise tumultuous game about grief . In this quiet aside, Esquie (an enormous, floating, and endearingly oblivious companion who’s arguably the emotional center of the whole game) is speaking to his dear friend Verso, one of the game’s traumatized playable leads. They are discussing their mutual friend François, who has gone quiet since losing his own closest friend. Verso mentions that François used to be all ‘wheee,’ but these days he’s a bit more ‘whooo.’ These are Esquie’s shorthand terms, we learn, for happy and sad. Already, this shows-not-tells us exactly how close these two are (we’ve all got baffling inside jokes turned vocab with our nearest and dearest) and allows us to feel immediately what it’s like inside their relationship. This is one of the realest-feeling moments in the game for me, despite everything going on in Expedition 33.

But Verso’s not done talking. He asks Esquie which of the two – ‘wheee’ or ‘whooo’ – is more Esquie’s vibe these days. Esquie does not pick. He’s whooo, sure, I mean, look at the world these characters are living through . But he is also wheee; he gets to tackle existential problems by spending time with his best friend, which is a lovely win. And this feels very realistic. Even when things are darkest, there’s usually something happening that we can hold onto, a little light to keep us feeling human and remind us that we’ll be okay.

It’s not surprising that such a simple yet resonant line came from a real-life emotionally nuanced moment. The game’s lead writer, Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, told Polygon back in May 2025 that this particular scene came together in the middle of the night , when she was too tired to do anything other than articulate the way the moment should sound. We’ve all been there, right? Life happens, and words fail us. We just sit back in our chairs and sigh. And communicate those feelings as best we can. And it feels so relieving, bonding, and right when the people around us just get what we’re trying to say, even when words fail.

So! Whatever the universe has in store for you today, remember you are both ‘whooo’ and ‘wheee.’ Perhaps you’re bracing for bad news that hasn’t landed yet, and you are ‘whooo;’ perhaps your pet will curl close to you on the couch later, and you shall be ‘wheee.’ Breathe deep through whichever happens first, allow yourself Esquie’s gift of perspective, and remember – You and me and Esquie: We’ve got this.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a "big mistake." We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what's next
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.
items.content:
Home Interviews Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a “big mistake.” We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what’s next Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.

Game Development , Interviews 2026-07-29 00:00 Genki 3 Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, offering a behind-the-scenes look at the development of 2025’s Game of the Year. After the presentation, AUTOMATON sat down with the developers to discuss their Japanese influences, their views on JRPGs, why Unreal Engine was the right choice for their small team, and why the studio has no intention of significantly increasing its headcount.

Participants are as follows: Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s views on physical disc production ending , check out part two of this interview.

—Could you tell me about the influence Japanese games and anime have had on your approach to game design? What were some of the biggest Japanese influences on Expedition 33?

Guillaume Broche: Growing up, I’d say 95% of the games I was playing were Japanese games, so I’ve always been super influenced by them. My first real video game memory was Final Fantasy VIII on PS1. Before that, I’d also played some games on the Mega Drive, but they were smaller titles and I don’t remember them very well because I was too young. But to this day, JRPGs in particular continue to be one of my favorite genres.

And of course, one of the main influences in my life is the Final Fantasy series and the work of Hironobu Sakaguchi, including titles like Lost Odyssey and Blue Dragon. Other JRPGs that have influenced me include the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series, the Atelier series, and Tales of Vesperia. I’ve said it a million times by now, but I pretty much play almost all JRPGs available at the time. Not every single one, but really a lot.

Obviously, Expedition 33’s gameplay is very much inspired by the older Final Fantasy games. It’s turn-based, and you have three characters facing three monsters, so they were definitely a massive inspiration.

Also, as I grew up, I think I’d been missing that kind of game ever since Lost Odyssey. Lost Odyssey was, for me, the last big realistic turn-based game. You still have titles like Yakuza and Persona coming out now, but they’re more stylized. On the other hand, I felt like the grand, epic, realistic kind of turn-based games like Final Fantasy X and Last Odyssey didn’t exist anymore. Since that’s my favorite type of game personally, I just wanted to make it.

—How about anime? I believe you’ve mentioned being a big Ghibli fan, but have you drawn influence from any specific titles?

Guillaume Broche: Yes, I know that for a lot of people in the West, Disney is a big part of their childhood memories, but for me, it’s Ghibli. Especially Spirited Away. I think I’ve seen that movie 50 times, no joke. It’s a masterpiece from A to Z, and I also love other films by the studio.

Also, I think one of the anime that inspired me for Expedition 33’s story was Attack on Titan. I really like the idea of a group of heroes fighting together, and I especially love the uniform. When you see any character from Attack on Titan, you instantly know they’re an Attack on Titan character because of the uniform. That’s something I really wanted to bring over into Expedition 33, making the game recognizable just from its uniforms.

In fact, I’m rewatching Attack on Titan right now because I haven’t watched it for at least six years. I’m on season four now, almost at the end, and really, it’s an absolute masterpiece for me.

Alan Reynaud: For the characters, there were a lot of anime that had a big influence on us. One of them is Bleach. I have to mention Bleach because the character designs in the series are spectacular. One of the things we took from it was designs that are super simple yet incredibly memorable. We wanted to have something like that, with a “rule of cool” approach. I’d say that was a big inspiration for the character creation.

items.title: "It's a sad decision." Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.
items.content:
Home Interviews “It’s a sad decision.” Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.

Interviews 2026-07-29 00:01 Genki 4 Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, where the developers shared technical insights into the making of 2025’s Game of the Year. Following the event, AUTOMATON sat down with the team and took the opportunity to ask about their thoughts on physical game releases. With PlayStation set to end game disc production in 2028, the developers briefly reflected on why they insisted on releasing Expedition 33 physically despite the added challenges, and discussed why they believe physical editions remain important to video games as a medium.

Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s Japanese influences, thoughts on Unreal Engine, and studio upsizing, check out part one of this interview .

— PlayStation recently announced that it will end physical disk production in 2028. What are your thoughts on that?

Guillaume Broche: Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores. And even if nowadays, I play mainly on PC myself, we have a lot of people on the team who play on PS5 and love to collect physical discs. I think it’s part of the beauty of art too – that it’s something tangible that you can touch. I completely appreciate that people want to have their rows of DVDs and games and just feel that they own them. So I think it’s a shame. I mean, business-wise, I can understand why it may make sense, but I think in terms of the artistry of video games, it’s a sad decision.

Tom Guillermin: In our discussions with our publisher prior to the release of Expedition 33, the question of whether or not to do a physical release cropped up. A physical release adds more constraints because you have to account for the production time of the physical items, and you also earn less money per copy.

But for us, physical was something special. We also felt that the game could be special to players, and that they would want to, as Guillaume said, hold it in their hands.

So even though it made things harder and meant less money per unit, it was important for us to provide players who want to have the physical game in their hands with an option. Because that’s what we value as players too.

Guillaume Broche: To add to that, there were two very strong moments when the game released. After launch, we went to a video game store to buy our own game (laughs). Just as a gesture. And another strong memory I have is when someone from Japan sent me a picture [of our game] from a video game store – in Akihabara I think – in Japanese writing and all. I felt like a kid when I saw it. I was like “Yeah, it’s real!” It starts feeling real when you see it in stores. Alan Reynaud: Even now when I’m going to the supermarket or something, if I see our game in a store, it always makes my day. It’s a bit selfish, because it’s our game, but it always makes me go “Oh!”

Knowing that may not be possible again makes me a bit sad. And maybe it’s the child in me, but I like to go outside, buy a game, and come back home with it. It’s a nice feeling.

Alexandre Breton: And it’s not just because it’s “our game.” I think what’s cool [about physical games in general] is that a few years later, you’ll have your box, and you can hold it and look at the title and remember all the memories that are linked to the game.

Alan Reynaud: I think the same principle can apply to manga. It’s nice to read on your phone and stuff, but having a real book is just a different feeling. And I don’t think we could imagine a world where manga is just scanned and stored on your computer. It would be sad to not have it in your library. I think the same applies for games. Sure, it makes more sense business-wise, but you lose the spirit of it.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available for PC ( Steam ), PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

items.title: Unreal Engine 5 Made Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Possible, Yet It Makes A Nintendo Switch 2 Port A Big Challenge
items.summary: Sandfall Interactive reveals how Unreal Engine 5 made Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 possible, but also how it makes a Switch 2 port challenging
items.content:
Since its launch in 2022, Unreal Engine 5 has been one of the most controversial game engines from Epic Games , mostly due to how demanding it is on PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series X , and PC , as well as the performance issues it brings. Although the engine has been significantly improved since , public perception hasn't changed much, with many gamers considering it one of the worst things to happen to modern gaming. However, many developers don't share this sentiment, as Sandfall Interactive , the studio behind the 2025 Game of the Year Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , couldn't have made the game without it.

"For starters, Unreal Engine has all the tools you need to make a game that looks big, even if you’re not a big team," Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Guillaume Broche said to Automaton . "And we were very lucky with the release timing of some of Unreal’s newer tools. Unreal Engine 5 itself came at the right time in production, then MetaHuman came at the right time, and so did Nanite and Lumen – everything came at the right time. So we were very lucky with that."

The best thing about Unreal Engine 5 is that it gives developers all the tools they need to make something great, Broche continued, while heaping praise on Blueprints , the visual scripting system that will eventually be deprecated in Unreal Engine 6 , once the new Verse/Scene Graph framework matures. "Blueprints, especially, are very important. Blueprints are like a visual scripting method that allows pretty much anybody in the team to write code thanks to how easy it is. It’s like chaining blocks together. In our studio, we have four programmers, but every game designer and every technical artist uses Blueprints to make game logic or environment logic, and that’s crucial for us to be able to ship this kind of game and this kind of quality."

Technical Artist Alexandre Breton also had only praise for Unreal Engine 5's Blueprints . "Blueprints are part of an ecosystem. It’s visual scripting, so it’s very ludic and you can learn it very easily. It’s part of an ecosystem because a lot of people are using it and sharing content, so you can also find resources like tutorials everywhere. You can also find Blueprint Packs and learn from them. People give them away for free or sell them, and it’s never too expensive. Overall, it’s a system that’s very cool to use."

Although several games powered by Unreal Engine 5 have made their way onto the Nintendo Switch 2 , Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has yet to do so. The team is interested in a port, but there are technical challenges that are even more daunting for a small studio like Sandfall Interactive .

"It’s a big technical challenge because we tried to do something beautiful with the game, but of course, the Switch 2 is not as powerful as the PlayStation or the Xbox Series X. So, it’s an important thing for us to consider, especially given the size of our studio," said studio Co-founder and CTO Tom Guillermin .

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 & the Beauty of a Non-Definitive Ending
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives Maelle and Verso two painful endings. This feature examines grief, escapism, and why neither choice is wrong.
items.content:
Imagine: it’s PAX West 2025, and you’re me, wandering the expo hall with hundreds if not thousands of others. It’s a sea of people, but amongst them, you start to notice an incredibly peculiar pattern: dotting the crowd are bright red French berets. You cross direct paths with someone and notice their red beret is not only accompanied by a black-and-white striped shirt, but a red checked sash, strapping a fake plastic baguette to their back. You’re immediately both intrigued and perplexed, and raise the obvious question to your partner, who explains it’s from that game he started playing “with Charlie Cox in it”.

In this scenario, you are very much a fan of Charlie Cox and his starring in Daredevil, so you’re immediately reminded of what he’s talking about in that explanation – Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. You vaguely remember seeing the first casting announcement trailer for it during a random State of Play one early morning and getting excited because Daredevil(!), but ultimately you ended up going back to your endless, hellish cycle of Marvel Rivals lobbies when the game actually released. The red berets are a kind reminder of your previous excitement about the game, though, and it isn’t long after that you find yourself glued to your television while being serenaded by a beautiful French accent as you are formally introduced to the citizens of Lumiere. Your four years of French classes throughout school surely prepared you for this moment.

What you aren’t prepared for is just how much of an effect this game has on you by the end.

Now, at the risk of being honest, it’s a complete understatement to say I love this game. If you have interacted with me within the last year, I have talked to you about this game, or I have told you to finish it after you told me you didn’t even get through Act I, or I have endlessly gushed over Lorien Testard’s soundtrack what was probably an annoying amount. It’s rare to find yourself so committed to a piece of media, if only because you see yourself reflected in it so wholly, whether it’s in Maelle’s escapism or Verso’s self-sacrificial tendencies. After all, you don’t win 37 awards because people just feel pretty okay emotions about your game. As is with any piece of media, though, comes what others have to say about it.

(Obligatory note: What’s discussed going forward is riding off of the notion that the person reading this has played the game. If you haven’t, maybe go open Steam or the PlayStation store, grab some tissues, strap in for a bit, and hopefully you will thank me later. Or feel free to keep reading – I’m certainly not stopping you).

One of the gaming community’s most divisive conversations regarding Expedition 33 is regarding the two distinct endings the game has to offer, notwithstanding how both are unique in how they highlight the game’s central theme around the idea of grief. There hasn’t been a day that’s gone by in recent memory where I haven’t been faced with someone explaining how “[insert your preferred character’s name] ending is the right one”, or “if you chose [insert your not-preferred character’s name] ending, you’re clearly heartless”.

In the first ending, the audience is brought back to Lumiere after Maelle and Verso’s battle, and we see that Maelle has not erased the canvas, which was her motivation by the end of Act III. We’re rejoined by the ensemble we’ve grown to love, the Expeditioners as well as Esquie and Monoco, and we even see that Gustave and Sophie have both been repainted after their previous deaths. We’re also faced with Maelle and a considerably older Verso. We see Verso struggle for an uncomfortable moment, his hands stretching out and freezing over keys of a grand piano in Lumiere’s opera house, until it can be discerned Maelle uses her Paintress abilities in order to force the painted version of her late brother to play.

The colors are washed. The lighting is dimmed. It doesn’t yield much comfort aside from the embrace of familiar faces, but that just might be enough.

The second ending is an intentionally stark contrast. For the first time in the game, we’re officially brought outside of the canvas now that it’s presumably been destroyed, as that was Verso’s desire by the end game, and we’re shown the Dessendre’s. In front of them sits a grave donning the name “Verso Dessendre”. Renoir and Aline share a tender embrace in front of their son’s grave, Clea leaves behind a bouquet of achingly familiar red and white flowers before excusing herself, and we see a scarred Alicia– or Maelle– standing by as she watches the scene unfold, holding a sewn Esquie doll. The camera turns and we see the images of the very same Expeditioners, including Gustave and Verso’s painted self, framed by the Eiffel Tower as they wave goodbye before dissipating.

The colors are bright. It’s backlit by a sunny day. The comfort is uncertain and bittersweet, but it’s ultimately not an unwelcome feeling, either.

Undeniably, the discussion around these endings is, of course, typically viewed as black-and-white as possible. More often than not, when faced with multiple endings by the end of a game, audiences are used to getting a “good” ending and a “bad” ending, leaving little room for discussion. And, in these cases, that is the game’s intent. In these cases, the games do have a black-and-white, a good-and-bad. It’s not unheard of for a game to punish a player for making poor choices throughout a play through. When looking at Expedition 33’s endings, though, this mindset is frankly doing a disservice to the game’s theming as a whole.

Grief as a theme is interwoven throughout the entire game, and when is the process of grieving ever black-and-white? Grief by all accounts is an incredibly non-linear process. We have all grieved over someone, over something, and we all understand what that means. Both of the endings evoke very different emotions, but it really is up to the player and what they choose to prioritize within their own grief. Yes, in Maelle’s ending, we see the way she chooses to use her Paintress abilities against her brother and father’s wishes, but more importantly, she’s also surrounded by those she has come to love, in a fully-functioning body. She’s given grace to those who have only ever lived inside of the canvas, reasserting the idea that they are sentient individuals with their own lives and autonomy, despite the circumstances they were painted into. Within Verso’s ending, the Dessendre’s are now able to work on moving past their shared grief regarding the loss of their real-life brother and son after years of stagnation, but at the cost of Alicia having a healthy physical body, and at the loss of everyone we have come to love inside of the canvas.

Both of these endings offer a resolution and catharsis in their own ways, and the outcome of one doesn’t make the other more or less right. When discussing these endings, we can’t assume why someone chose one ending over the other, because their grief surrounding the game is ultimately their own, and it’s not up to us to dictate how that feels to them. It can’t be stressed enough how sacrificing nuance in these discussions doesn’t only do a disservice to the game, but also the players and their own emotions about it.

I have a confession to make: I wholeheartedly chose Maelle’s ending the first time I played, and at that moment, it wasn’t a difficult choice for me. It made sense. I had grown so incredibly fond of Lumiere and the canvas and those inside of it, just like Maelle, but I saw myself in so many facets of her. I was a sixteen-year-old girl once, finding escape in worlds I created and in the media I was in love with, be it novels or games or movies, in order to remove myself from the very real grief I was experiencing. It’s something I still find myself doing even in adulthood, and ironically, probably the reason why I found myself so absorbed in Expedition 33 in the first place. The hours I put into the game were the direct result of me needing a distraction from life, and to watch the game slowly begin to unveil what it truly was felt like looking into a mirror. Of course I chose to save Lumiere. Of course I sided with Maelle. It’s what I do all the time. More often than not, I run from my grief rather than let myself feel it, and instead I look for reassurance and acceptance and comfort in worlds where my real feelings can’t hurt me. It’s far easier to feel for the characters on my screen than it is to feel for myself. After all, their emotions aren’t tangible, unlike my own. Expedition 33 was the first time I had ever personally experienced a piece of media that conveyed that feeling in a way that felt so specific, and so undeniably real.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is now available in Arabic!
items.summary: Expeditioners! Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text! This brings the total number of supported langua
items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Expeditioners!! Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special
items.content:
Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe? 

We’ve partnered with Orcival and Le Béret Français to bring you the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 striped shirt and beret for your cosplays! 🥖    You can purchase the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Orcival mariniere here

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team

  • Fixed facial hair of characters being blurred in the Photo Mode on the close distance if Shading was set to Epic.

    [/*]

  • Fixed an issue in Photo mode that prevented the Inner Cone Angle and Outer Cone Angle options from affecting the shape of the preview light source.

    [/*]

  • Photo Mode's spotlight and point light display has been modified to improve their visibility

    [/*]

Gameplay

  • Fixed an issue where loading a save while picking up a journal could cause that journal to disappear permanently and become impossible to collect again.

    • Missing journals are now also restored retroactively when loading affected saves.

      [/*]
    [/*]

  • Fixed a soft lock that could occur, during the Chromatic Glissando encounter in Sirene’s Dress level, when a dead expeditioner equipped with Shortcut and Second Chance pictos was swallowed.

    [/*]

  • Fixed an issue on Gestral Beach where using the Rematch option after losing the volleyball minigame could create a blocked save.

    [/*]

  • Fixed a visual issue where characters affected by Inverted would not have the correct colour effect applied to their eyes.

    [/*]

Environment

  • Fixed various environment issues (collisions, misplaced assets, missing or incorrect footsteps SFX) across Verso's Drafts, the World Map, and other levels.

    [/*]

  • Fixed various lighting issues on Steam Deck in Verso’s Drafts, Endless Tower and Stone Wave Cliffs levels.

    [/*]
